title: 1. The enterprise data warehouse
summary: The classic EDW: Inmon's Corporate Information Factory versus Kimball's bus architecture, built on MPP appliances and ETL tools with staging, ODS, warehouse and marts.

blocks.text: 37.1 Context and the problem it solved

By the late 1980s large companies ran dozens of operational systems: order entry, billing, inventory, HR, each with its own database and its own definition of *customer* and *product*. Reporting was done by running queries directly against those systems, which slowed down the applications and produced numbers that did not agree with each other. Every department had its own extract and its own spreadsheet truth.

The EDW answered three problems at once: **isolation** (analytical queries no longer hit production OLTP databases), **integration** (one conformed view of customers, products and time across systems) and **history** (operational systems overwrite state; the warehouse keeps it). Bill Inmon defined the warehouse as *subject-oriented, integrated, time-variant and non-volatile*, and that definition still describes what most gold layers try to be today (see chapter 15).

head: Aspect
Inmon: Corporate Information Factory
Kimball: dimensional bus architecture
rows: No separate central store; the conformed star schemas together are the warehouse
Dependent marts derived from the EDW
Business-process star schemas linked by conformed dimensions
Top-down: model the enterprise, then publish marts
Bottom-up and incremental: one business process at a time, guided by the bus matrix
Conformed dimensions and the enterprise bus matrix
Short; first mart in weeks to months
Dimensions drift apart if conformance is not enforced

blocks.text: In interviews, avoid framing this as a war with a winner. Most real EDWs were hybrids: a normalised integration layer (Inmon-like, later often Data Vault, see chapter 10) feeding conformed star schemas (Kimball-like) for consumption. The medallion model in chapter 12 is the same hybrid with new names.
37.2 Reference diagram

blocks.title: Classic EDW data flow
blocks.caption: Nightly ETL moves data left to right. The ODS is optional and sits beside the main path in many designs.

blocks.text: **Staging** is a landing zone: source extracts are copied as-is, usually truncated and reloaded each run, and never exposed to users. It exists so that extraction (hitting the source) and transformation (heavy work) can be separated in time; the source window is often only a few hours at night.

The **operational data store (ODS)** holds an integrated but *current* picture, refreshed frequently, for operational reporting such as 'orders placed in the last hour'. It is not historical. Many teams confuse it with staging; the difference is that the ODS is cleaned and integrated, and users do query it.

The **EDW** proper is the integrated, historised store. In CIF it is normalised and mostly hidden from end users. In the Kimball bus it is the set of fact tables and conformed dimensions themselves. **Data marts** are subject-specific subsets (finance, sales, supply chain), often with pre-built aggregates or OLAP cubes (Microsoft SSAS, Oracle Essbase, Cognos PowerCubes) for fast slicing.

blocks.text: **MPP appliances** were the hardware answer to growing data. A Teradata or Netezza system shards each table across many nodes by a distribution key, and each node scans its own slice in parallel (see chapter 5). Storage and compute are bought together as a rack, sized for peak load, with capacity planning cycles measured in quarters and costs in the millions. A badly chosen distribution key causes data skew, where one node does most of the work while the others wait.

**Where Iceberg, Snowflake and semantic models fit.** Iceberg did not exist; data lived in the proprietary storage of the appliance. Snowflake is the most common migration target for this architecture: the layers survive, the appliance disappears (chapter 26). Semantic models did exist, as OLAP cubes and BI universes, and they were often the most valued part of the EDW for business users; chapter 35 shows how today's semantic layers inherit that role.
37.4 Modelling and data layers in this architecture

head: EDW layer
Modelling style
Closest modern equivalent
rows: Bronze, but bronze usually keeps history; staging rarely did
Star schemas, SCD type 2 dimensions, aggregates

blocks.text: The Kimball **bus matrix** is the planning artefact: rows are business processes (orders, shipments, returns), columns are dimensions (date, customer, product, store), and a tick says the process uses that dimension. Every ticked dimension must be *conformed*, meaning identical keys and attributes wherever it is used. That single rule is what lets a report compare orders to returns by product without reconciliation.
37.5 Ingestion, orchestration and serving

Ingestion is **ETL**: transform before loading, on a dedicated ETL server, because warehouse compute was the scarcest and most expensive resource. A typical night looks like this: extract deltas from sources using timestamps or full dumps (log-based CDC arrived later, see chapter 17), land them in staging, apply lookups and surrogate-key assignment in the ETL engine, load dimensions first, then facts, then rebuild aggregates and cubes before the business day starts.

items: Extract window opens (for example 01:00) once source batch jobs finish.
Load staging tables, run row-count and checksum checks.
Process dimensions: detect changes, expire old SCD2 rows, insert new versions, assign surrogate keys.
Process facts: look up surrogate keys, route unmatched keys to an 'unknown' member or a reject table.
Rebuild aggregates and process cubes.
Publish: open the marts to users, usually by 06:00 or 07:00 local time.

blocks.text: The batch window is a hard constraint that grows worse with volume. When a load takes 6 hours and the window is 5, the warehouse is late every morning. Teams then add hardware, cut history, or skip validation; the last option is how silent data quality problems begin.
37.6 Strengths, weaknesses and failure modes

head: Strengths
Weaknesses
Typical failure modes
rows: One integrated, trusted version of key metrics
Long lead time for new sources or attributes (weeks to months)
Shadow IT: departments build their own marts in Access or Excel because the EDW queue is too long
Mature modelling discipline: conformed dimensions, SCDs
Expensive, coupled storage and compute; scaling means buying a bigger appliance
Load window overruns and late morning reports
Strong performance for known, structured queries
Poor fit for semi-structured, unstructured or high-volume event data
Big-bang CIF projects that run for years without usable output
Clear governance and ownership in a central team
ETL logic locked in a GUI tool repository: hard to version, test or review

blocks.text: 37.7 When to choose it / when not

items: **Choose it** when data is mostly structured, from a known set of operational systems, and the main consumers are finance and management reporting that require reconciled, auditable numbers.
**Choose it** when regulation or audit demands a single owner and controlled change of metric definitions.
**Avoid it** when large volumes of logs, events, images or JSON dominate and must be kept cheaply.
**Avoid it** when many independent domains need to ship data products without a central queue (see data mesh, chapter 43).
**Avoid it** when you need sub-minute freshness (see chapters 39, 40, 46).

**If you already run one**, plan a migration that keeps the model and moves the platform: lift marts to Snowflake or a lakehouse, rewrite GUI ETL as version-controlled SQL (chapter 31), replace cubes with a semantic layer.

blocks.title: A retailer's Teradata EDW, 2008 to 2024
blocks.text: A national retailer with 400 stores built a Kimball bus EDW on Teradata with Informatica ETL. Sales, inventory and returns marts shared conformed product, store and date dimensions, and the finance team closed the month from it. By 2020 the e-commerce clickstream (billions of rows per month) could not fit the appliance budget and was kept on a separate Hadoop cluster, so web and store sales were reconciled in spreadsheets. The appliance renewal quote forced a decision.
items: The team kept the bus matrix and all conformed dimensions as the target model.
Informatica mappings were rewritten as dbt models over Snowflake; around 30 percent were found to be dead and were dropped.
Clickstream landed in object storage as Iceberg tables and was joined to the same conformed dimensions.
SSAS cubes were replaced by a semantic model in the BI tool on top of the gold marts.

blocks.title: Draw the bus matrix for an insurer
blocks.text: An insurer wants an EDW covering policy sales, premium billing, claims and customer service calls. Draw the bus matrix (business processes as rows, candidate dimensions as columns). Decide which dimensions must be conformed, which processes would be your first two marts and why, and where you would put an ODS if claims handlers need same-day claim status reports.
hints: Think about which dimension appears in every row.
Policy and customer are related but not the same grain.
Ask what a claims handler needs versus what an actuary needs.

items: The EDW solved isolation, integration and history for structured operational data.
Inmon CIF builds a normalised enterprise store first; Kimball builds conformed star schemas one process at a time. Real systems are usually hybrids.
Staging is transient and source-shaped; the ODS is integrated and current; the EDW is integrated and historised; marts are consumer-shaped.
ETL ran outside the warehouse because warehouse compute was scarce; the nightly batch window was a hard limit.
The modelling ideas survive almost unchanged in cloud warehouses, lakehouses and semantic layers.

blocks.q: What is the main integration mechanism in a Kimball bus architecture?
options: An operational data store that every mart reads from
A normalised 3NF enterprise model that all marts are derived from
OLAP cubes that merge facts from different marts
Conformed dimensions shared across business-process star schemas
blocks.explain: Kimball integrates through conformed dimensions planned in the bus matrix. A normalised central model is the Inmon CIF approach, which is the tempting but wrong choice here.

blocks.q: How does an ODS differ from a staging area?
options: They are the same thing with different names
The ODS keeps full history; staging keeps only the current state
The ODS is integrated and queried for current-state operational reporting; staging is a transient, source-shaped landing zone
Staging is queried by users; the ODS is internal only
blocks.explain: Staging holds raw extracts for processing and is not exposed. The ODS is cleaned, integrated and current, and users do query it. It is usually not historical, so the claim that the ODS keeps full history while staging keeps current state is backwards.

blocks.q: Why did classic EDWs use ETL rather than ELT?
options: Warehouse compute on appliances was scarce and expensive, so heavy transformation ran on separate ETL servers
SQL could not express joins and aggregations at the time
Regulators required transformation outside the database
ELT is not compatible with star schemas
blocks.explain: The constraint was economic: appliance capacity was fixed and costly. SQL was perfectly capable of the transformations, which is why ELT took over once elastic cloud compute made in-warehouse processing cheap.

blocks.q: A company plans to migrate off a Teradata EDW. Which approach best preserves value?
options: Lift the appliance as a virtual machine into the cloud unchanged
Keep the conformed model and metric definitions, move storage and compute to an elastic platform, and rewrite GUI ETL as versioned code
Discard the dimensional model and land everything as raw JSON in a lake
Replace the marts with one wide table per source system
blocks.explain: The durable value of an EDW is its integrated model and agreed definitions; the weak parts are the coupled hardware and opaque ETL. Throwing the model away recreates the reconciliation problem the EDW was built to solve.
